title: Quantitative Locomotion Study of Freely Swimming Micro-organisms Using Laser Diffraction
protocol: Move 10-20 gravid adult nematodes to fresh NGM agar-filled Petri plates using a thin, flattened platinum wire pick.
Allow the nematodes to lay eggs for 3-5 hours and then remove the adults.
Incubate the Petri plates at 20 °C for 4-5 days to allow the nematodes to grow to early adulthood.
Flush a plate of young adult nematodes with 1 ml of deionized, distilled water.
Collect 50-150 worms from the synchronized culture.
Spin the worms to the bottom of the tube using a microcentrifuge or allow them to settle by gravity for about 15 min.
Remove the majority of the water and replace it with 1 ml of deionized, distilled water to wash any adhering bacteria from the nematodes.
Transfer nematodes in water or buffer to a quartz cuvette using a micropipette.
Work with a small number of nematodes, about 5-10 at one time.
Dilute the worms in water or buffer until a desired density is reached if necessary.
Pick individual nematodes to a drop of water or buffer on a fresh agar plate to wash them and transfer individual worms to the cuvette.
Perform setup using a 543 nm (green) Helium-Neon (HeNe) laser.
Place two front-surface aluminum mirrors to steer the laser beam through the cuvette.
Position a cuvette holder in the optical path of the laser beam.
Use a projection screen to capture the diffraction pattern of the organism.
Mount a high-speed camera capable of filming at ~240 fps to record the video.
Adjust the size of the cuvettes based on the study requirements.
Ensure the laser beam diameter is approximately 2 mm when interacting with C. elegans.
Maintain the laser beam diameter no larger than 5 mm to simplify diffraction pattern analysis.
Keep the distance from the diffracting organism to the screen much larger than the organism itself.
Place parafilm over the top of the cuvette.
Invert the cuvette to mix nematodes into the water column.
Place the cuvette in a holder so that worms are near the top initially.
Steer the laser beam through the center of the cuvette using mirrors.
Color the spot corresponding to the transmitted laser beam black on the projection screen.
Alternatively, put an opening in the projection screen for the transmitted beam to pass through.
Draw a 5 cm line on the projection screen next to the transmitted laser beam without interfering with the diffracted light image.
Start recording with the camera while room light is on.
Turn the room light off after starting the recording.
Record diffraction images of worms passing through the laser beam.
Install video analysis program on the computer.
Import the video into the video analysis program.
Set the origin to coincide with the transmitted laser spot.
Set the scale using the 5 cm line on the projection screen.
Track the angular displacement of the diffraction image formed by each nematode using the video analysis software.
Copy and paste data into a spreadsheet (Excel).
Add 180 degrees or π for all negative angles to produce a continuous graph.
Place a photodiode off center in the diffraction pattern right in front of the projection screen.
Connect the photodiode to the digital oscilloscope via USB port.
Observe the thrashing patterns on the computer screen.
Save acquired data sets in ASCII or text format.
Import the data into a data analysis program capable of fitting waveforms using chi-square minimization.
Fit a sinusoidal curve to determine thrashing frequency.
Take images of nematodes on a microscope slide using a traditional microscope.
Import the worm image 'Worm' into Mathematica by dragging the image into Mathematica.
Convert the image into a black and white image (binarize) with the 'Binarize' command in Mathematica: BlackandWhiteImage=Binarize[Worm].
Alternatively, use the 'EdgeDetect' command to create a BlackandWhiteImage: EdgeDetect[Worm,6.0,0.035], where the two trailing numbers control the coarseness of the resulting edges.
Convert the black and white image into a matrix of zeroes and ones with the 'ImageData' command in Mathematica: Matrix=ImageData[BlackandWhiteImage].
Use the 'Fourier' command in Mathematica to Fourier transform the matrix using the indicated FourierParameters: {0, -2}.
Square the absolute value of the matrix.
View the resultant image as the diffraction pattern corresponding to the original image.
Scale the contrast of the image using the 'Log' function.
Crop the central diffraction pattern.
Resize the image for easy viewing.
